chapters.summary: Jeremiah is called by God as a prophet, receiving visions and the message of both judgment and restoration.
keyPoints: God chose Jeremiah while he was still young, giving him the calling of a prophet.
God gives him words and visions, strengthening Jeremiah's courage to face opposition.
God declares that he will pluck up and break down, destroy and overthrow, but also build and plant.
chapters.application: Whatever our age or ability, God can use us. When he calls, he supplies the strength and promises we need to answer him boldly.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares God's charge against Israel's backsliding and idolatry, calling them to return and warning of the consequences of forsaking the true God.
keyPoints: God recalls Israel's first love, like the devotion of a bride, following him through the wilderness.
Israel forsook the fountain of living waters and dug for themselves broken cisterns that hold no water.
God rebukes Israel's sin, yet promises that if they return, they will find forgiveness and restoration.
chapters.application: Let us reflect on whether we have forsaken our first love, and turn back to God - he is the fountain of living water, ready to give us life and true satisfaction.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah calls backsliding Israel to return, promising that those who repent will find healing and restoration.
keyPoints: Like an unfaithful wife, Israel is still called by God to come home.
Judah saw Israel punished yet did not repent, making her hypocrisy all the more evident.
God promises that those who repent will receive shepherds and restoration, and be brought back to Zion.
chapters.application: However far we have strayed, God still calls us back in love. If we hear his voice today, let us humbly confess our sin, and he will cleanse us and lead us onto the right path.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah calls Israel to repent, warning that disaster from the north will come if they do not turn back, yet hope remains for those who return to God.
keyPoints: God calls Israel to return, to put away their idols, and to live with truth, justice, and righteousness.
He foretells disaster coming from the north like a lion or a scorching wind, because of the people's wickedness.
The prophet grieves for the people, yet shows that if they repent, Jerusalem can still be made clean.
chapters.application: When we drift from God in our own lives, remember that the door of grace to return still stands open. Walk in truth and righteousness, turn from evil, and mercy will meet us.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Jerusalem will surely be judged because no one does justice or seeks the truth; the people are stiff-necked and the prophets speak lies, so God will bring disaster upon them.
keyPoints: God searches for even one person who does justice, but finds none, revealing the corruption of the whole city.
The people reject God's discipline, stiffening their necks like senseless beasts.
The prophets and priests offer false peace, leaving the people trapped in sin and headed toward destruction.
chapters.application: Let us examine ourselves - are we truly doing justice and loving mercy, or following false teaching? May we live each day with honesty and reverence for God.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah warns the people of Judah that disaster is coming because they will not listen to God's word, yet God still calls them to repent.
keyPoints: Jeremiah announces that Jerusalem will be besieged, urging the people to flee to a fortified city.
The people refuse to listen to the prophet and do detestable things, and the prophet grieves for them.
God appoints watchmen, but the people will not listen, and in the end they are punished for their sin.
chapters.application: When God reminds us through his word and his Spirit, let us humbly obey and turn back in time, so that we do not miss the chance to receive his grace.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah preaches at the temple gate that Israel must not falsely trust in the temple but must truly repent and do justice, or else God will forsake this house as he forsook Shiloh.
keyPoints: God calls the people to amend their ways: do not steal, murder, oppress the sojourner, or follow after other gods.
False worship is worthless; the temple cannot become a hiding place for sin, or it too will be destroyed.
The people will not listen to God, and even the prophet's intercession is useless, because they have broken the covenant and judgment must come.
chapters.application: Do not rely only on outward religious form; examine your heart and your conduct, and treat others with honesty and justice - God delights in true repentance and obedience.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Judah's stubborn backsliding and false sense of peace will bring judgment, and he laments that the people will not repent.
keyPoints: God judges Judah, scattering their bones, because they worshiped idols and forsook him.
The people refuse to turn back, rushing headlong into battle like a horse, with no one repenting.
The prophet grieves for the people because they cling to a false peace and ignore God's warnings.
chapters.application: Let us turn away from false peace, face our sin honestly, and return to God in time, so that we may enjoy true peace.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah laments the sin and deceit of the people of Judah, calling them to know God and to practice justice, and foretells the judgment and sorrow that will come from not knowing him.
keyPoints: Jeremiah weeps over the people's sin, for they deal falsely and speak lies, refusing to know God.
God declares that because of their rebellion, their land will lie desolate and they will be scattered among the nations.
He calls the wise to understand God's will and glory in knowing him, foretelling the certainty of judgment and grief.
chapters.application: Let us glory in knowing God, put away falsehood and deceit, speak honestly in daily life, and rely on his justice and steadfast love for true security.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that the LORD is the true God and idols are worthless, urging the people to turn to him, and foretells the judgment of exile.
keyPoints: He rebukes the customs of the nations and the vanity of idols, which can neither bring good nor harm.
He praises the LORD as the only true God, who made the earth by his power and established the world by his wisdom.
He declares that Israel will be exiled for their sin, yet God will discipline them in measure and not utterly destroy them.
themes: The Greatness of the True God
chapters.application: Let us place our trust in the true God who created all things, turning away from every false support; even in discipline, let us still believe in his love and his plan.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares the covenant God made with Judah, warning that disaster will come if they refuse to obey, and exposes the plot to kill him.
keyPoints: God commands Jeremiah to remind the people of the covenant made at Sinai, stressing that obedience brings blessing and rebellion brings a curse.
The people of Judah have followed other gods and broken the covenant, so disaster will come upon them with no escape.
The men of Anathoth plot to kill Jeremiah, but God promises to punish them, for judgment is coming.
themes: The Prophet's Suffering and God's Protection
chapters.application: Let us hold fast to our covenant with God, living each day by his word as our standard; even when we face opposition, let us trust firmly that he watches over us and need not fear the schemes of others.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah pours out his complaint to God, asking why the wicked prosper; God answers by telling him to prepare for greater hardship, and declares both judgment and mercy on the rebellious people.
keyPoints: The prophet questions why the way of the wicked prospers, and asks God to execute justice.
God warns of the treachery of the people and their neighbors, and declares that disaster is coming.
God promises that in the end he will show mercy and bring the exiles back home.
chapters.application: When our hearts are troubled or we face hardship, let us trust in God's sovereignty - he will execute justice in his time and give us grace sufficient for the moment.

chapters.summary: Using the image of a linen waistband and wine jars, Jeremiah declares that Judah will be destroyed because of pride and idolatry, and calls the people to repent and return to God.
keyPoints: God tells Jeremiah to hide a waistband by the river Euphrates; when he retrieves it ruined, it pictures Judah's pride being destroyed.
The image of wine jars pictures judgment: the people will stagger against one another like drunkards, for their guilt is so great that God will show no pity.
The people are called to give glory to God, or else be punished, scattered before their enemies like sheep.
chapters.application: Let us humbly listen to God's word and turn back in time, before our hearts grow too hard to be moved. Examine yourself daily, and give glory to God.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah cries out to God over the drought disaster facing Judah, but God tells him not to pray for the people, because their sin must be punished.
keyPoints: A severe drought strikes Judah - the ground cracks, livestock die, and the people mourn.
The prophet intercedes, but God declares that disaster is coming because of the people's sin and the deceit of false prophets.
God commands Jeremiah not to intercede for the people, and foretells that sword, famine, and plague will destroy them.
chapters.application: When we face hardship, let us examine whether we have drifted from God, and truly repent - rather than only asking him to remove our suffering while refusing to change our lives.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah intercedes for Judah, but God declares that judgment is already settled; the prophet cries out over the suffering his ministry brings him, and God promises to strengthen him.
keyPoints: God refuses even the intercession of Moses and Samuel, because the people's evil deeds have brought destruction.
The prophet is hated by everyone for speaking God's word, and though his heart is in anguish, he remains obedient.
God promises to protect those who faithfully proclaim his word, and to punish those who persecute them.
chapters.application: When our prayers for others or our efforts to share the gospel are met with rejection, let us remember God's promise - he is with us, and he will deliver us.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah is commanded to remain unmarried as a sign to Judah that disaster is coming for their idolatry, yet God promises that in the last days he will gather them back from the lands of their exile.
keyPoints: God commands Jeremiah to remain unmarried, as a sign of the death and mourning about to fall on Judah.
Judah will be exiled and punished because they followed idols and forsook God.
God promises that in the future he will gather Israel and bring them home, giving them the grace to know him.
chapters.application: When circumstances seem hopeless, remember that God rules over history - he will judge in righteousness, and he will also restore in love. May we hold fast to faith in hardship, and wait for his deliverance.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Judah will be punished for their sin, but those who trust in the LORD will be blessed, and he calls the people to keep the sabbath holy.
keyPoints: Judah's sin is engraved with an iron pen, carved deep into their hearts, and must be punished.
Those who trust in man are cursed, but those who trust in the LORD are like a tree planted by water, and will surely be blessed.
The prophet asks God to heal and save him, and stresses the importance of keeping the sabbath holy.
chapters.application: Today let us examine our hearts, trusting fully in God rather than in human strength or circumstances, and honor the Lord's Day in worship, that we may find true rest and blessing.

chapters.summary: At the potter's house Jeremiah learns of God's sovereignty and mercy, declaring that Israel is like clay in God's hand, and calling them to repent.
keyPoints: God uses the image of the potter and clay to picture his sovereignty over Israel, free to shape or to break as he wills.
God warns that disaster will fall because of the people's evil, yet if they repent, he will relent and not bring it.
The people instead plot against Jeremiah's life, and the prophet asks God to judge them in righteousness.
chapters.application: Let us humbly submit to God's sovereignty, like clay in the potter's hand, always ready to be turned and renewed, and to receive his mercy.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah is commanded to smash a clay flask, a sign that God will destroy Jerusalem because Judah has worshiped idols and shed innocent blood.
keyPoints: God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay flask and gather the elders and priests at the Valley of Ben-hinnom to declare judgment.
Jeremiah declares that because Judah has forsaken God, worshiped false gods, and shed innocent blood, disaster is coming.
Jeremiah smashes the flask as a sign that God will break this people and this city, and because the people are stiff-necked and refuse to listen, judgment must come.
chapters.application: Let us turn away from idols and wickedness and listen to God's word - his warnings come from love, so may we turn back in time and receive his mercy.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah is beaten and put in stocks by the priest Pashhur for proclaiming God's message; he pours out his inner struggle and cries to God, yet still holds firm to God's presence with him.
keyPoints: The priest Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in stocks at the temple gate; Jeremiah declares that God will punish Judah and Pashhur himself.
Jeremiah cries out to God that he is mocked and reviled all day long, and even wishes he could stop proclaiming God's word, yet it burns in his heart like a fire he cannot hold in.
In his anguish Jeremiah still declares that God is with him like a mighty warrior, that those who persecute him will fail, and he asks God to vindicate him.
chapters.application: When we suffer persecution or ridicule for our faith, let us follow Jeremiah's example, entrusting our inner struggles to God, confident that his presence will bring us through.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Jerusalem will be attacked by Babylon because of her rebellion against God; he urges the people to surrender and live, and warns the royal house of Judah to do justice.
keyPoints: Jeremiah conveys God's will: the king of Babylon will take Jerusalem, and no one will be able to save it.
God urges the people to surrender to Babylon in order to survive, warning that those who resist will die by sword, famine, and plague.
If the royal house of Judah does justice, the throne of David will be established; if not, judgment will come.
chapters.application: When we face hardship, let us seek God's guidance, face it with a humble and obedient heart, and hold to justice, for God is sovereign over all things.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares God's judgment on the kings and people of Judah - because they do not act justly or listen to God's word, the temple and Jerusalem will be destroyed.
keyPoints: God requires the king to do what is just and right, or judgment will surely fall upon Judah.
Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim both come to tragic ends because of their wickedness.
Though Jerusalem is treasured, it will be laid waste because of the people's rebellion.
chapters.application: Let us uphold justice and honesty in our daily conduct, not seeking only our own gain. God sees everything and will repay each according to their deeds, so let us humbly obey his word.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah condemns the wicked shepherds (leaders) and false prophets, declares that God himself will gather the remnant, and promises to raise up a righteous Branch - the offspring of David - who will bring justice and salvation.
keyPoints: God will punish the shepherds who ruin and scatter his flock, and he himself will gather his sheep.
He rebukes the false prophets who speak in God's name yet proclaim false visions, leading the people astray.
He promises that the Branch of David (Christ) will reign as king, executing justice and righteousness, and bringing salvation to Judah.
chapters.application: Let us be watchful against false teaching and hold fast to God's word. Even in the midst of chaos, God still reigns; he will personally watch over his people and give us the hope of righteousness.

chapters.summary: Using the image of two baskets of figs, Jeremiah declares that those taken into exile will be restored, while those who remain in the land will face disaster.
keyPoints: God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs, one very good and one very bad.
The good figs represent the exiles of Judah, whom God will watch over and bring back home.
The bad figs represent Zedekiah and his people, who will suffer sword, famine, and plague.
chapters.application: In hardship, let us trust in God - his discipline is mingled with mercy, and those who return to him will be restored; let us not imitate the rebellious, but respond to God with humble obedience.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Judah will be carried into a seventy-year captivity in Babylon for not listening to God, after which Babylon itself will be punished, for God will judge all nations.
keyPoints: God rises early to send his servants to warn the people, but they will not listen.
Judah will be exiled to Babylon for seventy years, after which Babylon will be punished.
God makes all the nations drink the cup of his wrath, a sign that judgment is coming upon every land.
chapters.application: Let us turn back while God still offers grace, and not harden our hearts. God rules over history and will surely judge in righteousness - let us trust his promises and hold fast to hope.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah proclaims God's message of judgment in the temple and is opposed by the priests and false prophets, but the officials and the people protect him, and in the end he is spared death through the support of Ahikam.
keyPoints: Jeremiah, commanded by God, proclaims in the temple court that if the people do not repent, the temple will become like Shiloh and Jerusalem will be cursed.
The priests and false prophets seize Jeremiah and demand his death, but the officials and the people decide he does not deserve to die.
Jeremiah's life is spared through the protection of Ahikam, and he reaffirms that his message is from God, calling the people to repent.
chapters.application: When truth is opposed, let us still proclaim it boldly, trusting that God protects the faithful. Today, let us hold fast to the truth and not shrink back because of circumstances.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares, by God's command, that the nations must serve King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and reject the lies of false prophets, or else disaster will surely come.
keyPoints: God has handed the nations over to the king of Babylon; those who submit will be preserved, but those who resist will face sword and famine.
The prophet rebukes false prophets who preach peace and mislead the people, urging them not to believe such empty lies.
The vessels of the temple will be carried off to Babylon, and only be returned on the day God visits his people.
chapters.application: When circumstances seem difficult, discern God's voice and refuse false comfort. Submit to what God has ordained, wait for his promise, and find hope in patient endurance.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah confronts the false prophet Hananiah in the temple; Hananiah predicts the yoke of Babylon will soon be broken, but Jeremiah warns that true peace comes only in God's own time.
keyPoints: Hananiah prophesies that within two years the yoke of Babylon will be broken, and Jeremiah responds before all the people.
Jeremiah points out that whether a prophecy comes to pass is the true test of a prophet.
Hananiah breaks the wooden yoke, but Jeremiah foretells his death, and it comes to pass that same year.
chapters.application: When we face false comfort, let us stand firm on the word of God, wait patiently for his promises, and refuse to follow human lies.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah writes to the Judahites exiled in Babylon, urging them to settle down and seek peace in a foreign land, promising their return after seventy years, and warning them against false prophets.
keyPoints: He urges the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, and multiply in Babylon.
God promises that after seventy years he will visit them and bring them back to their homeland, giving them peace and hope.
He warns them not to listen to the lies of false prophets and diviners, for they will surely be punished.
chapters.application: In hard times, settle in and work faithfully, trusting that God has his own timing and plan. His thoughts toward us are thoughts of peace, and he will surely lead us toward hope.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares God's promise to bring exiled Israel and Judah home, healing their wounds and giving them peace and hope.
keyPoints: God promises to bring Israel and Judah back from captivity, restoring their land and their worship.
The day of the LORD will bring great distress, but God will save his people and break their yoke.
God will heal his people's wounds and build them up, so that they will be his people and he will be their God.
chapters.application: Whatever hardship we face, God watches over his people and promises restoration and healing. Let us wait patiently in hope, trusting his faithfulness to lead us into peace.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah 31 declares that God will rebuild Israel and give a new covenant, changing hearts from within, forgiving sin, and restoring an intimate relationship with him.
keyPoints: God promises that Israel and Judah will be rebuilt, gathered again in grace.
He declares the new covenant, in which his law is written on the heart and all will know him.
God forgives their sin and remembers it no more, and his people enjoy peace and joy.
chapters.application: The new covenant is already written on our hearts. Let us rely on the Spirit each day, experience God's forgiveness and renewal, and respond to his love with joy.

chapters.summary: During the siege, Jeremiah buys a field at God's command, a prophetic sign that Judah will be exiled yet will ultimately return and be restored.
keyPoints: At God's command, Jeremiah buys the field at Anathoth from his cousin Hanamel, signing and sealing the deed and weighing out the silver as legal proof that the land will one day be redeemed.
God declares he will punish the people for their sin, but promises to rebuild and replant them and to make a new covenant with them.
God, who created heaven and earth by his mighty power, finds nothing too hard for him, and he will surely fulfill the restoration he has promised.
chapters.application: God still reigns in the midst of hardship. His promises never fail; let us act in faith, confident that he will lead us into restoration.

chapters.summary: In prison, Jeremiah receives God's promise of restoration, declaring that Jerusalem will be healed and made prosperous again, and that a righteous Branch of David will arise.
keyPoints: God promises to reveal himself to Jeremiah once more, displaying his power and faithfulness.
Though Jerusalem has been destroyed, God will heal and rebuild it, and forgive its sin.
The covenant with David will stand firm; a righteous Branch will reign, and the Levitical priests will never lack a man to serve.
chapters.application: When circumstances seem hopeless, remember that God holds tomorrow, and his promises never fail. Call upon him in prayer, and he will show you great and hidden things.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Jerusalem will fall to Babylon, yet promises that Zedekiah will die in peace; he also condemns Judah for breaking the covenant to free their slaves, which brings disaster.
keyPoints: Jeremiah prophesies that Jerusalem will be taken by Babylon, and that Zedekiah, though captured, will die in peace.
Judah frees its Hebrew slaves and then goes back on its word, breaking God's covenant and bringing punishment upon itself.
God declares judgment of exile, sword, famine, and plague upon them because they did not keep the covenant.
chapters.application: God values the integrity of our promises; we must not go back on our word. Let us deal honestly and faithfully with others, for God will judge according to our deeds, yet he also grants grace to those who repent.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah uses the Rechabites' faithfulness to their ancestor's command as an example to rebuke the people of Judah for not listening to God's word, and promises the Rechabites a blessing.
keyPoints: God tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into the temple and offer them wine, but they refuse because of their forefather's command.
Jeremiah uses this to contrast Judah's failure to listen to God's word, which brings disaster upon them.
God promises that because of their obedience, the Rechabites will always have a man to stand before him.
chapters.application: Let the Rechabites be our example - faithfully obeying God even in the small matters of daily life, so that we too may find his favor and blessing.

chapters.summary: At God's command, Jeremiah writes his prophecies on a scroll; King Jehoiakim burns the scroll, but God commands it be rewritten, showing that his word cannot be destroyed.
keyPoints: Jeremiah dictates, and Baruch writes down the LORD's words, intending to read them in the temple.
When King Jehoiakim hears them, he cuts up the scroll and burns it, then seeks to seize Baruch and Jeremiah.
God commands Jeremiah to rewrite the scroll and declares judgment against the king.
chapters.application: Though God's word may be rejected or destroyed, it endures forever. Let us reverence and obey Scripture, never treating it lightly because of circumstance, but treasuring and proclaiming it.

chapters.summary: When Babylon's siege is briefly lifted, Jeremiah prophesies that it will return; he is then imprisoned for leaving the city, yet still urges surrender and foretells the city's fall.
keyPoints: Zedekiah inquires of Jeremiah, but the king will not listen to the LORD's word and only hopes the siege will lift.
Jeremiah prophesies that the Babylonians will surely return and burn the city with fire.
Though imprisoned, the prophet continues to declare God's word, showing his faithfulness.
chapters.application: Even when circumstances seem to improve, hold fast to God's word. Do not drift from the truth because of present comfort - remain faithful to the end.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy cistern for prophesying Jerusalem's destruction, then rescued through Ebedmelech's plea, and once again delivers God's message to King Zedekiah.
keyPoints: The officials accuse Jeremiah for preaching the LORD's word and have him thrown into a cistern full of mud.
Ebedmelech, acting in faith, pleads with the king and has men pull Jeremiah out of the mud with ropes.
Jeremiah privately urges King Zedekiah to surrender to Babylon to save his life, but the king hesitates, fearing the Judeans.
chapters.application: When we face hardship or misunderstanding, let us hold fast to the truth like Jeremiah, and reach out courageously to help others like Ebedmelech. Trust that God watches over the faithful.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah 39 records the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, the capture of King Zedekiah, and the exile of the people of Judah - while Jeremiah himself is released and protected, fulfilling God's prophecy.
keyPoints: Babylon captures Jerusalem; King Zedekiah is seized, his sons are killed before his eyes, and his own eyes are then put out.
Jeremiah is released from the guard's courtyard and handed over by the Babylonians to Gedaliah, given his freedom.
Through Jeremiah God foretells disaster upon Judah, but promises that the obedient will be spared, as Ebedmelech is delivered.
chapters.application: When circumstances seem hopeless, remember that God governs history and his promises will surely be fulfilled. Let us obey his word and look to his deliverance in suffering, finding true peace.

chapters.summary: Set free, Jeremiah chooses to remain with Gedaliah and comfort the remnant at Mizpah, marking a new beginning for the remnant of Judah.
keyPoints: Jeremiah is freed by Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, and chooses to stay in Judah.
Gedaliah is appointed governor and urges the people to submit to Babylon so they may live in peace.
The remnant of Judah gathers at Mizpah and begins the harvest, while Ishmael's plot quietly takes shape.
chapters.application: In times of upheaval, let us seek God's guidance and choose to submit to what he has ordained, holding on to hope even in ordinary life, for he cares for his people.

chapters.summary: Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah, plunging the people into panic; Johanan pursues the killer and plans to flee to Egypt.
keyPoints: Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah and many others of Judah, breaking his oath and sowing chaos.
Johanan leads his forces in pursuit and rescues the captives, but Ishmael escapes.
Fearing Chaldean reprisal, Johanan decides to lead the remnant down to Egypt.
chapters.application: In times of turmoil, let us seek God's guidance rather than make decisions out of fear. Even when the way is dark, God still reigns, and he watches over those who trust him.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah warns the remnant of Judah not to go down to Egypt, but they disobey and go anyway, bringing disaster upon themselves.
keyPoints: The remnant of Judah asks Jeremiah to inquire of God's will and promises to obey whatever he says.
Jeremiah declares God's word: if they stay in the land they will have peace, but if they go down to Egypt they will meet sword and famine.
The leaders and the people refuse to listen and insist on going to Egypt, rebelling against God.
chapters.application: Let us truly seek God and be willing to obey his guidance, never saying one thing and meaning another, lest we stray from the right path and suffer loss.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah warns the remnant of Judah not to flee to Egypt, but they refuse to listen and force him and Baruch to go with them; Jeremiah then prophesies that Babylon will strike Egypt.
keyPoints: The leaders of Judah reject Jeremiah's warning from God and insist on going to Egypt.
The people carry Jeremiah and Baruch away with them into Egypt, defying God's will.
Through Jeremiah, God declares that Babylon will invade Egypt and that judgment will surely come.
chapters.application: When our own plans conflict with God's will, let us humbly seek him rather than act on our own judgment. Only in submission to God can we find true peace.

chapters.summary: In Egypt, Jeremiah declares the LORD's judgment on the remnant of Judah, for they persist in idolatry and will surely meet disaster and destruction.
keyPoints: Jeremiah delivers God's word to the Judahites who fled to Egypt, warning them never to worship idols again.
The people refuse to repent and insist on worshiping the queen of heaven, provoking God's wrath and disaster.
God points to history as witness, showing that their own and their ancestors' evil brought desolation upon Judah, and still they will not repent.
chapters.application: Let us remind ourselves to turn away from every form of idolatry and obey God's word. Even in adversity, let us turn back to God, and he will surely show mercy.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah delivers God's message to Baruch, comforting him in his suffering, telling him not to seek great things for himself, and promising to spare his life.
keyPoints: Baruch is grieved by the prophecy, and God comforts him through Jeremiah.
God will tear down what he has built and uproot what he has planted, yet he promises to preserve Baruch's life.
Baruch must not seek great things for himself, and he will be kept safe amid the disaster.
chapters.application: In hard times, do not seek great things for yourself, but set your heart wholly on God, and he will surely keep you to the end.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares God's judgment on Egypt, prophesying that Egypt will be defeated by Babylon, yet promising that Israel will ultimately be saved.
keyPoints: God uses Babylon to judge Egypt, showing that he governs the destinies of the nations.
Egypt's pride will be brought low, and its army, though mighty, will prove no match.
Though Israel is punished, God promises that in time they will return from captivity.
chapters.application: When the world seems ever-changing, let us humbly rely on God, for he governs history; and even through discipline, let us trust that he will grant the grace of restoration.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah prophesies that the Philistines will be struck by Babylon like a flood, for the day of the LORD is near and the whole land will be destroyed.
keyPoints: The disaster against the Philistines is foretold: Babylon comes from the north like a flood, sweeping over the whole land.
Wailing and destruction: the sword devours the Philistines; parents wring their hands, powerless to save even their own children.
The day of the LORD: God has decreed the disaster, and even the remnant of the Philistines will perish.
chapters.application: When disaster comes, let us humbly rely on God, for he governs all things and his justice will surely be made known.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Moab will be destroyed because of its pride and self-reliance, yet God promises to restore Moab's fortunes in the last days.
keyPoints: Because of its pride and complacency, Moab despises God and will surely face disaster and shame.
Moab's towns and people will be laid waste by sword and plunder, with no one escaping.
Though God judges Moab, he promises that in the last days he will restore its captives.
chapters.application: Beware of pride, and humbly rely on God; even in suffering, remember that he is merciful and will restore us in the end, giving us hope.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares God's judgment on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, and Hazor and the other nations, showing that God governs all the nations, and promising that Israel will ultimately be restored.
keyPoints: God judges Ammon for occupying Israel's land, but promises its eventual return.
Edom, for its pride and self-deception, will be brought very low and left uninhabited.
Damascus, Kedar, Hazor and other cities will be destroyed and their people scattered.
chapters.application: Do not grow proud in a moment of ease, but humbly rely on God; even under discipline, he remains merciful, preparing a way out for those who repent.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Babylon will be destroyed for its pride and wickedness, while Israel and Judah, though exiled, will surely return and be forgiven.
keyPoints: Babylon, for its pride and cruelty, will face God's judgment, struck down like a bull of Bashan.
Israel and Judah are like scattered sheep, but God promises to bring them home and forgive their sin.
Babylon's idols and false gods are powerless, and its land will lie desolate, without inhabitant.
chapters.application: When pride or wrongdoing has carried us away from God, remember that he is both just and merciful. He will lead us to repent and return, giving us forgiveness and new life.

chapters.summary: Jeremiah declares that Babylon will be destroyed by God's judgment, and calls on God's people to flee it, showing that God governs the history of every nation.
keyPoints: God raises up an enemy against Babylon to overthrow it, repaying it for its wickedness.
He calls Israel to leave Babylon, lest they share in its punishment, and to turn back to God.
He declares that Babylon's idols are useless, and that the LORD alone is the true God who governs all things.
chapters.application: When the world tempts us to drift from God, let us stay alert to his justice and turn back without delay, refusing to love the world, and following him in faith to find peace.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the tragic history of Judah's final king Zedekiah's rebellion, the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, the destruction of the temple, and the exile of the people.
keyPoints: Zedekiah rebels against Babylon; Jerusalem is besieged, and when the city falls the king is captured, his sons killed before his eyes, and his own eyes then put out.
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon burns the temple and the palace, tears down the city walls, and carries the people into exile, leaving only the very poorest behind.
The temple's bronze pillars, the bronze sea, and other vessels are seized; the priests and leaders are put to death, and the people of Judah are carried away to Babylon.
chapters.application: This history reminds us that turning away from God brings discipline, but his promises never fail. Let us live in reverent obedience to God, holding on to hope even in the midst of hardship.
